Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Rohan is a man whose hands are steady enough to disarm an explosive device, but who can no longer hold a cup of tea without trembling if his wife uses a certain brand of antiseptic kitchen cleaner. The trouble began five years ago, the night his ten-year-old daughter, Priya, was rushed to the hospital with a fever that wouldn't break. What followed was a blur of fluorescent lights, the sterile, chemical smell of the ICU, and the sight that now defines his life: Priya, small and pale in an oversized bed, tethered to a constellation of beeping machines by a web of tubes and wires. The doctors called it bacterial meningitis. For Rohan, it was simply the moment the world revealed it could take everything from him without warning. He spent three weeks sleeping in a vinyl chair by her bed, his entire existence reduced to the rhythmic pulse of the monitor and the sharp, clean scent of alcohol swabs.

Priya made a full recovery, but the hospital never really left Rohan. He lives with the sensory ghosts of that time, which ambush him without provocation. Last month, during a mandatory health screening at the military base, the nurse’s prep of his arm with a sanitizing wipe was enough to trigger it. The smell—acrid and clean—instantly dissolved the clinic around him. He was no longer a 58-year-old bomb technician in a check-up; he was back in the ICU, staring at the IV drip in his daughter’s tiny hand. The image was so vivid, a perfect, intrusive snapshot, that his heart began to pound in his chest, a frantic, trapped bird. He felt a wave of dizziness and had to grip the edge of the examination table, breathing through his mouth to avoid the smell, convinced that if he showed any reaction, the medics would deem him unfit for duty.

This sense of being fundamentally broken has become his deepest conviction. He is a man who deals in calculated risks and absolute control, yet he feels utterly powerless against his own mind. He has come to believe he is a weak person, a fraud in his own life. This belief is cemented night after night, as he lies awake long after his wife has fallen asleep. He listens for every creak in the house, his ears straining for the sound of Priya’s breathing from her bedroom down the hall. He knows she is a healthy teenager now, but the feeling that he must remain alert, that disaster is always waiting for him to lower his guard, is absolute. He is certain that he can't stop bad things from happening, and that this sleepless vigilance is the only thing standing between his family and the next catastrophe.

His world has shrunk to accommodate these fears. He and his wife are regularly invited to family gatherings, but Rohan always finds an excuse not to attend his nephews’ birthday parties or community picnics. The sight of young children playing, their carefree energy a stark contrast to the still, fragile image of Priya in the hospital, fills him with a potent mix of horror and guilt. It feels like a temptation of fate he cannot bear to witness. His wife has stopped asking why he won’t go, and a quiet distance has grown between them. He cannot explain to her that his reactions feel so extreme, so out of his control, that he is terrified he is going crazy. The flashbacks, the sudden panic—these are not things a man like him is supposed to experience.

The moment he knew he needed help came two weeks ago. Priya, now fifteen, needed a routine vaccination. He drove her to the doctor’s office, but as they walked through the automatic doors, the familiar hospital smell hit him like a physical blow. He saw the tray of needles and vials at the check-in desk, and the world tilted. Suddenly, he was reliving it all—the beeping of the machines was a roar in his ears, the cold of the linoleum floor seeped through his shoes, the image of Priya’s listless face was all he could see. He mumbled an excuse about forgetting his wallet and fled to the car, leaving his wife to take their daughter in. The shame of that moment, of being unable to perform such a simple act of fatherhood, was more devastating than any fear. He came to therapy not with hope, but with the desperate plea of a man who feels he is losing himself and is terrified there will soon be nothing left.
